clinicalPearls: SCA42 is an autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia caused by mutations in CACNA1G, which encodes the pore-forming alpha-1G subunit of the Cav3.1 low-voltage-activated (T-type) calcium channel.
A recurrent missense variant, p.Arg1715His, accounts for many reported families and tends to produce a relatively consistent, slowly progressive ataxia.
Typical adult-onset features are gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and cerebellar eye signs such as gaze-evoked nystagmus and saccadic pursuit.
Pyramidal signs, tremor and sometimes peripheral sensory disturbance may accompany the cerebellar syndrome, so the phenotype ranges from nearly pure to mildly complex.
More disruptive, often de novo CACNA1G variants cause a distinct, severe early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder with cerebellar atrophy, contrasting sharply with the milder classic adult SCA42.
Cav3.1 T-type channels drive rhythmic low-threshold firing in cerebellar and thalamic circuits, so their dysfunction disturbs cerebellar output.
MRI shows cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with pontine involvement in more severe cases.
reference.pathophysiology: SCA42 is caused by heterozygous mutations in CACNA1G on chromosome 17q, which encodes Cav3.1, the alpha-1G pore-forming subunit of a T-type (low-voltage-activated, transiently opening) voltage-gated calcium channel. Cav3.1 is strongly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje and granule cells, the inferior olive and the thalamus, where it underlies rhythmic burst firing and pacemaking. The recurrent p.Arg1715His substitution lies in a voltage-sensing segment and shifts the voltage dependence of channel activation, altering calcium influx and neuronal excitability through a change-of-function effect that disturbs cerebellar signalling and drives Purkinje cell dysfunction and cerebellar atrophy. More severe, frequently de novo variants cause larger functional disturbances and underlie the early-onset neurodevelopmental phenotype associated with the same gene.
additionalDifferentials: SCA6 (CACNA1A) — a related calcium-channel dominant ataxia, slowly progressive and relatively pure
SCA15/16 (ITPR1) and SCA11 (TTBK2) — dominant pure cerebellar ataxias
Episodic ataxia type 2 and other channelopathy-related ataxias
Congenital or early-onset cerebellar ataxias with developmental delay, for the severe de novo CACNA1G phenotype
Sporadic adult-onset cerebellar ataxia and the cerebellar variant of multiple system atrophy
additionalInvestigations: CACNA1G sequencing by single-gene test, ataxia panel or exome, reporting the recurrent p.Arg1715His variant where present
Exclusion of the common repeat-expansion ataxias
Brain MRI to assess cerebellar and, where relevant, pontine atrophy
Nerve conduction studies if peripheral involvement is suspected
Parental testing to confirm a de novo origin in early-onset or apparently sporadic cases
Family pedigree analysis, genetic counselling and cascade testing
redFlags: Early-onset ataxia with developmental delay, epilepsy or dysmorphism suggests the severe de novo CACNA1G phenotype and alters prognosis and counselling.
Rapid deterioration or autonomic failure suggests an alternative diagnosis such as the cerebellar variant of multiple system atrophy.
Prominent seizures or marked cognitive regression warrant reassessment of the diagnosis.
reference.prognosis: Classic adult-onset SCA42 is slowly progressive, with mobility usually preserved for years; the severe early-onset neurodevelopmental form associated with CACNA1G carries a substantially poorer outlook.
pitfalls: Conflating the mild adult SCA42 with the severe de novo neurodevelopmental CACNA1G disorder, which differ greatly in prognosis.
Assuming a normal expansion panel excludes a dominant ataxia and not proceeding to gene sequencing.
Missing a de novo origin by not testing parents in apparently sporadic early-onset cases.
Overlooking the recurrent p.Arg1715His variant when only large structural changes are sought.
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists for this CACNA1G-related ataxia, so centre care on physiotherapy for gait and balance, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy
Institute falls prevention and provide mobility aids for gait and limb ataxia
Treat tremor symptomatically and apply antispasticity measures for pyramidal features
Monitor for bulbar dysfunction with periodic swallow assessment
For the severe, often de novo early-onset neurodevelopmental form, provide early developmental intervention and paediatric multidisciplinary care
Offer genetic counselling with parental testing to confirm a de novo origin in early-onset or apparently sporadic cases and define recurrence risk
